answers.brief_reasoning: Defensible claim grounded in sleep science.
answers.final_answer: Yes. A district should move high school start times later, because later starts let adolescents get more sleep, and more sleep improves attention and learning.

answers.brief_reasoning: Experimental evidence on sleep and attention.
answers.final_answer: Source 1: students randomly assigned to 8 hours in bed scored 85% mean accuracy on an attention task, compared with 71% for students given 6 hours. The difference was statistically significant.

answers.brief_reasoning: Link via sleep deprivation and selective attention; random assignment gives a causal inference.
answers.final_answer: Source 1 used random assignment, so it shows that sleep restriction itself causes worse selective attention. Sleep deprivation impairs the ability to focus on relevant stimuli (the targets) and ignore distractors. Attention is the first step of encoding information into memory (information processing model), so sleep-deprived students would encode less of what they hear in class. A later start that allows more sleep should therefore improve attention and learning.

answers.brief_reasoning: Survey links later start to more sleep.
answers.final_answer: Source 2: students in the district starting at 8:45 a.m. reported an average of 7.6 hours of sleep on school nights, compared with 6.4 hours in the district starting at 7:15 a.m.

answers.brief_reasoning: Circadian rhythm phase delay in adolescence; note the correlational limit.
answers.final_answer: During puberty, adolescents' circadian rhythm shifts later (a phase delay in melatonin release), so they naturally fall asleep later. With an early start time they cannot simply go to bed earlier, and they build up a sleep debt. A later start fits their biological clock, which matches Source 2's 1.2 extra hours of sleep. The survey is correlational, since districts were not randomly assigned and may differ in things like family income, but the finding fits what circadian research predicts. More sleep also supports memory consolidation, which happens during deep sleep and REM sleep, and that benefits learning.
